title: Honey-Walnut Baked Pears with Cinnamon
dek: Firm pear halves turn tender and caramel-edged in the oven, with toasted walnuts tucked into their centers and a warm cinnamon-honey glaze spooned over every serving.
image_alt: Two golden baked pear halves filled with walnuts and glazed with honey on a white plate
ingredients: 2 tbsp unsalted butter, melted, plus more for the baking dish

instructions.name: Heat the oven and prepare the dish
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 375°F with a rack in the center. Lightly butter a 9-by-9-inch or similar 2-quart baking dish; choose one that holds eight pear halves in a snug single layer without stacking.

instructions.name: Halve and core the pears
instructions.text: Halve the pears lengthwise, leaving the stems attached where possible. Scoop out each seed core with a teaspoon or melon baller, making a 1 1/2-inch-wide hollow without cutting through the base. Brush every cut surface with the lemon juice and arrange the halves cut-side up in the dish.

instructions.name: Mix the cinnamon-honey glaze
instructions.text: Whisk the melted butter, 2 tablespoons honey, vanilla, cinnamon, ginger and salt in a small bowl. Brush the mixture over the cut sides and into the hollows, then turn the pears cut-side down. Pour the hot water around—not over—the fruit.

instructions.name: Steam-roast until almost tender
instructions.text: Cover the dish tightly with foil and bake for 20 minutes. Carefully remove the foil and turn the pears cut-side up with a thin spatula. They should be beginning to soften but still hold their shape.

instructions.name: Fill with walnuts and finish uncovered
instructions.text: Divide the walnuts among the pear hollows and spoon the buttery pan juices over the fruit. Bake uncovered for 12 to 15 minutes more, until the edges are golden and a paring knife slides into the thickest part with little resistance. If the pears are very firm, continue in 3-minute increments rather than increasing the oven temperature.

instructions.name: Glaze and serve
instructions.text: Rest the pears for 5 minutes so the juices thicken slightly. Stir the remaining 2 tablespoons honey into the warm pan juices, then spoon the glaze over the pears and walnuts. Serve two warm halves per person, with any extra glaze from the dish.

why_it_works: Bosc pears retain their shape under heat, so the halves become spoon-tender without collapsing before the walnuts toast.
A covered first stage traps steam from the measured water and softens the dense fruit evenly before browning begins.
Turning the pears cut-side up for the second stage exposes their edges to dry heat while protecting the walnut filling from a full 35 minutes of roasting.
Lemon tempers the honey's sweetness and slows surface browning while the pears are being prepared.
Stirring the final honey into warm pan juices produces a glossy finishing glaze that matches the visible plated dessert without scorching the honey in the oven.
swaps: Use firm Anjou pears if Bosc are unavailable. Begin checking 5 minutes early because Anjou pears can soften faster depending on ripeness.
Replace the walnuts with pecans in the same quantity. For a nut-free version, use 1/3 cup toasted pumpkin seeds and confirm the package meets your allergy needs.
Use refined coconut oil or a plant-based butter in place of dairy butter for a dairy-free dessert; the glaze will have a slightly different aroma.
Maple syrup can replace the honey measure for a vegan version. The glaze will be thinner, so rest the pan juices for 2 extra minutes before spooning them over the fruit.
storage: Cool leftovers within 2 hours and refrigerate the pears with their glaze in a shallow airtight container for up to 4 days. Reheat covered at 325°F for 12 to 15 minutes, until hot in the center, or microwave one serving at 50% power in 30-second intervals. Spoon the glaze over the fruit again after reheating. Freezing is not recommended because thawed pears release water and lose their clean halved shape.
notes: Choose pears that yield only slightly at the neck. Fully soft pears can collapse before their cut edges caramelize, while rock-hard pears may need 6 to 10 extra minutes.
A melon baller makes a neat hollow, but a metal measuring teaspoon works just as well. Remove only the fibrous core; leaving a thick fruit wall prevents leaks.
Keep the hot water around the pears rather than washing the seasoning off their cut surfaces. The liquid should not cover the fruit.
Calories and cost include two pear halves, 2 tablespoons walnuts and one quarter of the glaze per serving; actual values vary with pear size and local prices.
Honey should not be served to children younger than 12 months. Use maple syrup when preparing a portion for that age group.

faqs.q: How do I know baked pears are done without making them mushy?
faqs.a: Insert a thin paring knife into the thickest part near the stem end. It should slide in with little resistance while the pear still holds a defined edge. Test at 32 minutes and add only 3 minutes at a time because ripeness changes the exact baking time.

faqs.q: Can I assemble honey-walnut pears ahead?
faqs.a: You can halve, core and season the pears up to 4 hours ahead; cover the dish and refrigerate it without the hot water. Add the water just before baking. Chop the walnuts separately and add them only for the uncovered stage so they stay crisp.

faqs.q: What can I serve with baked pears?
faqs.a: They are complete as pictured with walnuts and glaze. For a richer dessert, add plain Greek yogurt, lightly whipped cream or vanilla ice cream at the table rather than in the baking dish; those additions change the calories and are intentionally optional so the finished pears remain photo-accurate.
